s: The English 'consciousness' for viññāṇa entered Abhidhamma study through a definitional move that carried Victorian psychology with it: Shwe Zan Aung (1910) matches Anuruddha's division to Bain's Feeling, Will and Intellect and defines mind as 'that which is conscious of an object' before deriving 'consciousness' for viññāṇa; such English is evidence for 1910, not for the antiquity of the concept.

src.q: The vedanā-ñāṇa-saṅkhāra-bheda¹ of our author, however, corresponds to Bain’s division of the mind into Feeling (vedanā), Will, or Volition (saṅkhāra or cetanā), and Thought or Intellect (ñāṇa).

src.q: Mind is, then, ordinarily defined as that which is conscious of an object.

s: Slingerland and Chudek (2011), counting pre-Qin uses of xin (heart/heart-mind), report that xin alone of the organs was regularly contrasted with the body and that in the Warring States it became less tied to emotions and more the unique locus of 'higher' cognition; on this reading neither 'heart-mind' holism nor a single English word fits all periods, and Legge's 'feeling' (Mencius 2A6) and Xunzi's thinking ruler sit at different points of a shift.

s: Interpretive, tested on the pages: the 17th-century turn that makes awareness (conscientia) the mark of the mental (Descartes 1641/1644) arrives together with its counter. The page that gives English philosophy 'consciousness' (Cudworth 1678) coins it to name what plastic nature LACKS and attacks the Cartesian equation of cogitation with consciousness; Leibniz's apperception is defined against unnoticed perceptions. But the awareness criterion is older than the turn: Ficino (1482) already defines sensing as the soul's act not escaping its notice, and Agrippa makes perception wait on reason's turning.

s: Brentano (Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte I, 1874, Bk II ch. 1 §5) characterises every psychical phenomenon by what the Scholastics called the intentional (or mental) inexistence of an object, the direction toward an object, and says this is peculiar exclusively to psychical phenomena: the mark of the mental becomes object-directedness, not a soul-substance.

src.l: Franz Brentano, 1874, Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte, Bd. 1
src.q: This intentional inexistence is peculiar exclusively to psychic phenomena. No physical phenomenon shows anything similar.

s: Brentano (1874, Bk II ch. 1) reports Hamilton's objection that feelings of pleasure and pain have no object: in them 'consciousness (das Bewusstsein) does not set the psychic state before itself' but is fused with it; an early form of the later split between object-directed and merely felt (phenomenal) states.

src.l: Franz Brentano, 1874, Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte, Bd. 1

s: Huxley (1874, 'On the hypothesis that animals are automata', as quoted by James, Principles I, 1890) makes the consciousness of brutes a collateral product of the body's mechanism, as powerless over it as a locomotive's steam-whistle, extends this to men ('We are conscious automata'), and says the soul stands to the body as a clock's bell to its works, consciousness being the sound.

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: as completely without any power of modifying that working as the steam-whistle which accompanies the work of a locomotive engine is without influence on its machinery

s: Clifford (quoted by James, Principles I, 1890) holds that physical and mental facts are 'on utterly different platforms', run in parallel without interference, and that saying the will influences matter is 'nonsense'.

src.l: William James, 1890, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I
src.q: The two things are on utterly different platforms—the physical facts go along by themselves, and the mental facts go along by themselves.

s: Du Bois-Reymond (Über die Grenzen des Naturerkennens, 1872, as quoted by Steiner 1901) asks what conceivable connection there is between motions of atoms in the brain and 'I feel pain, ... see red', and calls it forever incomprehensible that it should not be indifferent to atoms how they lie and move; Steiner sums it up: for knowledge there is no bridge from motion to sensation (Empfindung).

s: Haeckel (Die Welträthsel 1899, Eng. 1901, ch. on consciousness) reports that Du Bois-Reymond's Leipzig address of 14 August 1872 named two absolute limits of natural knowledge, matter-and-force and consciousness (how substance 'comes, under certain conditions, to feel, to desire, and to think'), and rejects this 'transcendental (dualistic)' view for a 'physiological (monistic)' one.

s: James (Human Immortality, 1898) argues that the brain's 'production' of consciousness is as much a metaphysical hypothesis as its 'transmission', since science has no conjecture of the process either way, and quotes the physiologists' 'Ignoramus, ignorabimus' and 'the late Berlin professor' (Du Bois-Reymond) calling the production of consciousness in the brain the absolute world-enigma.

src.l: William James, 1898, Human Immortality: Two Supposed Objections to the Doctrine
src.q: Ignoramus, ignorabimus, is what most physiologists, in the words of one of their number, will say here.

s: James ('Does "Consciousness" Exist?', 1904) denies that 'consciousness' names an entity or stuff while insisting it names a function, knowing; he calls the word, evaporated into Bewusstsein überhaupt, 'the faint rumor left behind by the disappearing "soul" upon the air of philosophy'.

s: James (1904) says that in himself the 'stream of thinking' is chiefly the stream of breathing, and that Kant's 'I think' that must be able to accompany all objects is 'the "I breathe" which actually does accompany them'; breath, 'the original of "spirit"', is what philosophers built consciousness out of.

src.l: William James, 1904, Does 'Consciousness' Exist?

s: The passage of Bucke's Cosmic Consciousness (1901) reprinted in Ouspensky's Tertium Organum (Eng. 1922) ranks three grades of consciousness: simple consciousness (the upper animals), self-consciousness (man, able to treat his own mental states as objects), and cosmic consciousness, a higher form possessed by a few: 'consciousness' has become a ladder one can climb.

s: Chalmers (1995) separates the 'easy' problems of explaining cognitive functions from the 'really hard problem' of experience, asks why information-processing does not go on 'in the dark', and, citing Nagel 1974 and Levine 1983, says an account of functions stays on one side of an explanatory gap.

s: Block (1995) calls consciousness 'a mongrel concept' and separates phenomenal consciousness (experience, what it is like to be in a state) from access consciousness (availability for reasoning and the rational guidance of speech and action).

src.l: Ned Block, 1995, On a confusion about a function of consciousness

s: Tononi (2004) proposes that consciousness corresponds to a system's capacity to integrate information, so that it is a fundamental, graded quantity present in infants and animals and buildable in artefacts; a photodiode differentiates light from dark but generates minimal information and presumably does not 'see'.

src.l: Giulio Tononi, 2004, An information integration theory of consciousness

s: Hacker (2012) argues that 'consciousness' is a latecomer to Western philosophy: the ancients' sunoida and conscio meant 'I know together with (another)' or 'I know well', ancient and medieval thinkers discussed inner senses but did not characterise the mind as the domain of consciousness.

src.l: P. M. S. Hacker, 2012, The Sad and Sorry History of Consciousness: being, among other things, a Challenge to the 'Consciousness-studies Community'

s: Heller-Roazen (The Inner Touch, 2007) writes the history of 'the sense of being sentient' from Aristotle's power by which animals perceive that they perceive, through the Greek, Arabic, Hebrew and Latin common sense likened by one ancient author to an 'inner touch', to the modern notion of consciousness.

src.l: Daniel Heller-Roazen, 2007, The Inner Touch: Archaeology of a Sensation

s: Turing (1950, §6(4)) answers Jefferson's 'argument from consciousness' (no machine could feel, not merely signal, pleasure or grief) by saying its extreme form is solipsism, since one could be sure a machine thinks only by being it, and he relies on 'the polite convention that everyone thinks'; he adds that he does not deny there is a mystery about consciousness.

src.l: A. M. Turing, 1950, Computing Machinery and Intelligence

s: Against reading the 'hard problem' as new in 1995: the same question, why moving matter should feel at all, was stated as an absolute limit of science by Du Bois-Reymond in 1872 ('I feel pain ... see red'), was answered by Huxley's epiphenomenal steam-whistle (1874), turned by James into the 'Ignorabimus' of 1898, and anticipated by Fechner's dead clock that 'sees nothing from within' (1860); what is new in 1995 is the word 'experience' carrying it without the word 'soul', which these writers still used.

s: An open letter of 124 researchers (2023) argues that IIT's implications (an inactive grid of logic gates may be conscious, possibly more than humans; early fetuses, organoids, perhaps plants) are untestable, and that given its panpsychist commitments the pseudoscience label should apply until the theory as a whole is empirically testable.

s: Seth (2025) challenges the assumption that computation suffices for consciousness, arguing that consciousness depends on our nature as living organisms (biological naturalism), so that real artificial consciousness is unlikely along current trajectories: the functionalist premise of the indicator approach is the contested step.

s: Interpretive, refining the soul concept's seed: in the Platonist line experience is split four ways, not three: the composite or the spirit is affected (pathos); the soul, or 'we', apprehends that affection (antilēpsis), and that apprehension is an act, not a suffering; following one's own act (parakolouthēsis) is a further, optional reflection that can be absent or even dim the act; and the soul itself is not acted on. Impassibility is a claim about being affected, never about lacking awareness.

s: Interpretive: the English philosophical word 'consciousness' was born defining an absence. Cudworth (1678) introduces it as a gloss on Plotinus' synaisthēsis in order to say what plastic nature, a life that forms plants and animals, does NOT have, and on the same page rejects the Cartesian equation of thought with consciousness; Leibniz's apperception is likewise defined against perceptions without it. From its first page the word named the difference between a working process and the same process felt.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The True Intellectual System of the Universe: the first part

s: Interpretive: the 'hard problem' is not the soul/sensation split with the soul removed, but the older split between doing and undergoing with the doer mechanised. In Sāṃkhya the buddhi acts and is not conscious while the puruṣa undergoes and never acts; in Cudworth plastic nature works without consciousness; Fechner's dead clock 'sees nothing from within'; Du Bois-Reymond (1872) calls the step from moving atoms to 'I feel pain' forever incomprehensible; Chalmers (1995) asks why processing does not go on 'in the dark'. What 1995 adds is the name and the separation of the 'easy' functional problems, not the question.

s: Interpretive, for the machine argument: three traditions set the same test for when representing becomes experiencing. Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta say light that holds every reflection but lacks self-grasping (vimarśa) is an inert crystal; Fechner's self-coinciding dead clock sees nothing from within; Plotinus' activity without its mirror goes on unapprehended. In each, what is missing is a reflexive turn of the process on itself, which is also what the higher-order and attention-schema indicators in Butlin et al. (2023) try to operationalise.
